title: CAS reads allocate attacker-sized objects before verification

attack_path_facts.title: CAS reads allocate attacker-sized objects before verification
attack_steps: A lower-trust contributor supplies an adopted or preseeded .kcs store containing an attacker-sized, hash-consistent CAS object and a hash or ref that selects it.
The operator invokes inspect or a HEAD/tree consumer against that supplied store.
ObjectStore::read_by_hash validates hash syntax but calls fs::read at crates/kcs-core/src/cas.rs:78-100 before digest, kind, JSON-shape, or command-specific size validation.

The victim process allocates, reads, and hashes all N bytes; raw inspect at crates/kcs-core/src/scope.rs:623-637 retains the full object merely to report its size, while poisoned refs can repeat the primitive in routine repository commands.
assumptions: The victim adopts the supplied store and invokes a command that selects the object.
The contributor can provide a valid SHA-256 name or a supplied ref for the oversized object.
The object is large enough relative to victim memory and I/O capacity to cause substantial disruption.
attack_path_facts.context: Copied, shared, and preseeded stores are explicitly untrusted at adoption. The issue crosses that supplied-state boundary into the KCS process's resources, but remains a local, scope-bounded availability defect.
attack_path_facts.in_scope: yes; adopted-store parsing and CAS boundedness are covered by I6, I7, and I12
attack_path_facts.exposure: not public; local filesystem artifact consumed through operator-invoked CLI commands
attack_path_facts.identity: KCS reads as the operator's OS user; the lower-trust contributor needs pre-adoption control of the supplied store, not write access to the victim's private live store.
attack_path_facts.cross_boundary: yes: untrusted adopted CAS state deterministically controls victim allocation and hashing, though no confidentiality or privilege boundary is crossed
preconditions: Adoption of a lower-trust copied or preseeded store
A supplied hash/ref and an inspect, HEAD, tree, or related consuming command
attack_path_facts.attacker_control: yes over the supplied object bytes, size, hash, and store refs; no control over the victim process identity is required
attack_path_facts.category: unbounded CAS object allocation and local denial of service
mitigations: Hash syntax and fixed fan-out paths are checked before lookup.
SHA-256 equality is verified after the read.
Kind and JSON validation protect integrity after allocation.
attack_path_facts.impact_surface: runtime memory, I/O, CPU, and repository-command availability
attack_path_facts.target_reach: one adopted scope and each command that selects the oversized object or poisoned ref
counterevidence: The contributor must supply a hash-consistent object, so arbitrary false-hash garbage is rejected.
Resource use is approximately linear in bytes already present in the supplied store rather than a small-input amplification.
Direct same-user mutation of an already private live store is out of scope.
The bounded control proved full allocation but intentionally did not measure peak RSS or force OOM.
blindspots: Practical exhaustion thresholds and packaging of very large supplied stores were not measured.
No end-to-end poisoned-HEAD stress case was run.
controls: Stream digest verification with a bounded buffer.
Apply per-kind byte and cardinality ceilings before allocation.
Implement metadata-only raw inspection without retaining complete object bytes.
attack_path_facts.rationale: Hard suppression does not apply because the threat model recognizes a lower-trust supplied-store contributor distinct from private-live-store authority. The substantial but local and recoverable availability impact is Medium; adoption, object size, and command-selection prerequisites constrain likelihood to Medium. The matrix yields Low/P3.

Direct same-user mutation of an already private live store is out of scope.

proof_gap: Practical exhaustion thresholds and packaging of very large supplied stores were not measured.
